title: What Size AC Do I Need for My San Diego Home?
h1: What Size AC Do I Need for My House in San Diego?
description: How to figure out what size AC your San Diego home needs: how sizing works, why square footage alone fails, and what a proper load calculation looks at.
quick_answer: The right AC size depends on more than square footage. A proper load calculation looks at insulation, windows, sun exposure, ceiling height, duct location and whether you're near the coast or inland. Two homes the same size in San Diego can need different systems. A contractor should calculate it rather than match the old unit.
body:
What does AC size actually mean?

AC size is about cooling capacity, not physical size. It's measured in BTUs per hour or in tons. One ton equals 12,000 BTUs per hour of cooling. Most homes have systems somewhere in the range of a couple of tons up to five tons, depending on size and how much heat the house picks up.

The goal is to match the system's capacity to how much heat your home gains on a typical hot day. Too small and it can't keep up. Too big and it causes a different set of problems.

Why can't you just use square footage?

Square footage rules of thumb are a quick starting point, but they miss most of what makes a home hot. Two 1,800-square-foot homes can need very different systems if one has an insulated attic, shaded windows and a coastal breeze, and the other has thin insulation, big west-facing windows and sits in an inland valley.

Things that change the load include:

  • Location. Coastal neighborhoods stay mild, while inland areas like East County and North County inland valleys see much hotter summer afternoons.
  • Insulation and air sealing in the attic and walls.
  • Windows: how many, which direction they face, and whether they're single or double pane.
  • Ceiling height and two-story layouts.
  • Duct location. Ducts in a hot attic gain heat before the air reaches your rooms.
  • Shade, roof color and how many people live in the home.

What happens if an AC is too big?

An oversized AC cools the house quickly and shuts off before it runs long enough to pull moisture out of the air. That's called short-cycling. The house can feel cool but clammy, especially near the coast. Frequent starts also wear out parts faster, and rooms far from the system can stay warm because the unit never runs long enough to reach them evenly.

Bigger also costs more to buy and can require larger ducts than your home has.

What happens if an AC is too small?

An undersized system runs nonstop on hot afternoons and still can't reach the thermostat setting. It may do fine on a mild day near the coast, then fall behind during an inland heat wave or a Santa Ana event when temperatures spike. Constant running means higher bills and more wear.

How does a contractor calculate the right size?

The industry standard is a load calculation, commonly done with a method called Manual J. The contractor measures the home and enters details about construction, insulation, windows, orientation and local climate. The result tells you how much cooling and heating the home actually needs.

A good contractor will also:

  1. Inspect the ducts and check that they can deliver the airflow the new system needs
  2. Look at the return air size, which is often undersized in older homes
  3. Ask which rooms are uncomfortable now
  4. Consider whether a variable-speed system or zoning would help a two-story home

Be cautious of a quote that matches the old unit's size without any measurements. The old system may have been the wrong size all along.

Does heating matter when sizing an AC or heat pump?

For a straight AC, cooling load drives the size. If you're choosing a heat pump, the contractor also needs to check the heating load. Coastal winters are mild, but inland nights can get cold, and a heat pump sized only for cooling might need backup heat on the coldest mornings. A good load calculation covers both so the system is comfortable year-round.

Can insulation or duct work change the size you need?

Yes. Adding attic insulation, sealing air leaks and sealing or replacing leaky attic ducts can lower your cooling load. Sometimes that means a smaller, less costly system will do the job. If you're planning attic or duct work, do it before or with the AC replacement so the system is sized for the improved house.

For homes with a few hard-to-cool rooms, like a converted garage or upstairs bonus room, a ductless mini-split can handle that area without upsizing the whole system.

faqs: How many tons of AC do I need for a 2,000 square foot house?

It depends on the home. Insulation, windows, sun exposure, duct location and whether you're coastal or inland all change the answer, so two 2,000-square-foot homes can need different sizes. A load calculation is the only reliable way to know. Be wary of anyone who sizes by square footage alone.
Is a bigger AC better in a hot area?

No. An oversized system cools in short bursts, doesn't remove humidity well, and wears out faster. Inland homes do often need more capacity than similar coastal homes, but the right size comes from a load calculation, not from going bigger to be safe.
Should my new AC be the same size as my old one?

Not necessarily. The old system may have been sized incorrectly, or your home may have changed with new windows, added insulation or a room addition. A new load calculation tells you what the home needs now.
Can a mini-split help instead of a bigger AC?

Often, yes. If one or two rooms are hard to cool, like a bonus room over the garage or a converted garage, a ductless mini-split can handle that space directly. The main system can then be sized for the rest of the house.
